extracted.intended_audience: regulators, policy analysts, administrative law scholars, and practitioners evaluating public comments and rulemaking processes
extracted.subtask_description: A rubric for assessing the substantive contribution and quality of public comments submitted during notice-and-comment rulemaking, emphasizing outcome-oriented criteria (effectiveness, efficiency, equity) rather than participant satisfaction. Useful for agencies and researchers who must judge which comments improve rule quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Did the comment lead to a rule that achieved its statutory objective at lower cost or higher benefit than alternatives? A good comment improves outcomes, not just process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess comments by whether adoption would advance substantive ends (improved outcomes). Do not equate participant satisfaction or consensus with effectiveness; use outcome-focused evidence and plausibility of causal link between the comment and better policy. (Coglianese warns the MTBE consensus example: agreement among stakeholders did not prevent a harmful outcome.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Did the comment surface information that reduced decision costs (e.g., by identifying a problem that would have required later correction)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value comments that save agency resources by preventing foreseeable implementation problems, narrowing issues, avoiding rework, or clarifying technical matters that would otherwise require costly follow-up. Look for specificity and timeliness of the information provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity
rubrics_metrics.description: Did the comment introduce or address distributional concerns the agency would have missed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether comments raise distributional impacts or represent perspectives of groups likely to be excluded from elite stakeholder consensus. Consider whether the comment identifies who wins/loses under proposals and suggests mitigations for disproportionate harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce information unavailable to the agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce information unavailable to the agency (not just signaling preferences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for new factual data, empirical evidence, technical expertise, or practical knowledge (e.g., on implementation or local conditions) that meaningfully expands the agency's decision-making baseline. Distinguish such substantive inputs from pure preference statements or advocacy signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify implementation pitfalls / downstream problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify implementation pitfalls the agency might not see (the MTBE-style downstream problems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize comments that foresee how a rule will operate in practice and warn of unintended consequences, monitoring gaps, enforcement difficulties, or downstream harms. Use the MTBE groundwater contamination example as an anti-pattern: negotiated consensus failed to detect downstream harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface excluded perspectives for equity reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Surface excluded perspectives that should be considered for equity reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value comments that bring in voices or concerns absent from elite stakeholder discussions—especially those representing vulnerable, local, or marginalized communities—and that explain how proposals differently affect subpopulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propose changes that reduce cost or increase benefit (cost-effectiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose changes that reduce overall regulatory cost or increase regulatory benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the concreteness and plausibility of suggested alternatives: do they materially change expected costs or benefits? Prefer proposals with evidence or mechanisms explaining how they improve cost-effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the "consensus trap"
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the 'consensus trap' — recognizing that broad agreement may reflect captured discussion rather than good policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat broad agreement among elite commenters with caution; consensus can signal stakeholder capture or narrow framing. Reward disruptive or contrarian comments that surface overlooked risks or perspectives, and use independent analysis rather than consensus alone to validate policy quality.
